identification.summary: Pinstripe Lightning is Microsoft's current name for an actor cluster whose public aliases in Microsoft's mapping include Arid Viper, Desert Falcons, Scimitar, RENEGADE JACKAL and the legacy element name NIOBIUM [S1]. Under the Arid Viper / APT-C-23 / Desert Falcon names, vendors describe an Arabic-speaking, politically motivated espionage group that uses Windows and Android malware, mainly against Middle Eastern targets [S2][S3][S5]. Cisco Talos assessed with high confidence that Arid Viper was responsible for the Micropsia activity it reported and said the group is believed to operate from Gaza [S3]. This record rests on vendor reporting under the Arid Viper names; no Microsoft-authored report on Pinstripe Lightning was retrieved [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky said Desert Falcons began developing operations in 2011, with real infections from 2013 and activity peaking in early 2015 [S2]. SentinelOne and others describe activity since at least 2017 under the Arid Viper name [S5]. Talos dates the Micropsia malware to 2017 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Pinstripe Lightning. Microsoft's mapping lists NIOBIUM (legacy), RENEGADE JACKAL, Desert Falcons, Scimitar and Arid Viper [S1]. NIOBIUM differs by one letter from NOBELIUM (Russian actor, now Midnight Blizzard); they are unrelated. Vendors also use APT-C-23 for Arid Viper [S3][S5]. Cybereason's Operation Bearded Barbie report called APT-C-23 a sub-group of Molerats, and said its infrastructure was almost entirely separate from known APT-C-23 infrastructure; press coverage attributed the same campaign to Arid Viper [S4]. Keep Molerats / Gaza Cybergang as a separate cluster unless Microsoft states otherwise [S4][S5].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is confirmed in the sources gathered. SentinelOne says Arid Viper is suspected to operate on behalf of Hamas but that further conclusive information is needed [S5]. Kaspersky said in 2015 that the Desert Falcons operators are likely native Arabic speakers with apparently political motivation, and did not publicly tie them to a specific state [S2]. Microsoft's origin field for this record is blank in the source data.
attribution.confidence: Vendor-level, not government attribution. Talos: high confidence that Arid Viper was responsible for the Micropsia campaign it reported, and that the group is believed to operate from Gaza [S3]. ESET: medium confidence attribution of the AridSpy campaigns to Arid Viper [S6]. SentinelOne: Hamas link suspected, needs further evidence [S5]. Cybereason attributed Operation Bearded Barbie to a Hamas-linked Molerats sub-group (APT-C-23), a different framing from press reports naming Arid Viper [S4].
attribution.basis: Malware lineage and lure content (Micropsia, politically themed Palestinian documents) [S3]; Android spyware code and infrastructure overlaps assessed by ESET [S6]; linguistic and targeting assessment by Kaspersky [S2]; SentinelOne's alignment assessment [S5].

objectives: Espionage and information theft against political, government, military, law-enforcement and activist targets, primarily in the Palestinian territories, Israel, Egypt and the wider Middle East [S2][S3][S4][S6]. Kaspersky assessed the Desert Falcons motivation as political [S2].

regions: Wider Middle East; Kaspersky also saw victims in the US, Russia, France and Sweden [S2]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky reported more than 3,000 victims in over 50 countries and over one million files stolen in the Desert Falcons campaign, with most victims in Egypt, Palestine, Israel and Jordan [S2]. Talos reported a wave from about October 2021 using lures reusing Anadolu and Palestinian MA'AN content against Palestinian entities [S3]. Cybereason reported Facebook catfishing of Israeli defense, law-enforcement and emergency-services personnel [S4]. ESET reported victims in Palestine and Egypt, with most Palestinian detections tied to a fake civil registry app [S6].

capabilities.summary: Kaspersky described proprietary Windows and Android tooling in 2015, and a Unicode right-to-left trick that reverses displayed file names to disguise executables [S2]. Talos documents the Delphi-based Micropsia malware, run since 2017, delivered with politically themed decoy documents [S3]. Cybereason documented the Barb(ie) Downloader and BarbWire backdoor, delivered through fake social media personas and a RAR lure [S4]. SentinelOne describes actively maintained tooling across Delphi, Go, Python and C++, and Android malware (SpyC23) spread via weaponized apps posing as Telegram or a dating app [S5]. ESET documented AridSpy, a multistage Android spyware downloading first- and second-stage payloads from its C&C server, delivered via trojanized messaging apps, a fake Palestinian Civil Registry app and a job app, distributed from third-party sites and not Google Play [S6]. Social engineering and phishing with themed lures are the common entry methods [S3][S5].

campaigns.name: Desert Falcons disclosure
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky announced the group on 18 February 2015 as the first known Arabic-speaking cyber-espionage group, estimating at least 30 operators in three teams and more than 3,000 victims across 50+ countries [S2].

campaigns.name: Micropsia wave against Palestinian targets
campaigns.summary: Talos reported a new Micropsia wave starting around October 2021 using politically themed lures against Palestinian entities and activists, assessed with high confidence as Arid Viper [S3].

campaigns.name: Operation Bearded Barbie
campaigns.summary: Cybereason reported fake Facebook personas used against Israeli defense, law-enforcement and emergency-services personnel, delivering the BarbWire backdoor; Cybereason tied it to Hamas-linked APT-C-23 / Molerats while press named Arid Viper [S4].

campaigns.name: AridSpy Android campaigns
campaigns.summary: ESET described five Android campaigns beginning in 2022 using trojanized apps against users in Palestine and Egypt, attributed with medium confidence; three were still active at publication on 13 June 2024 [S6].

campaigns.name: SentinelOne Israel-Hamas war cluster review
campaigns.summary: SentinelOne listed Arid Viper among Hamas-aligned clusters, citing an IDF report of a campaign against soldiers near the Gaza border suspected to be Hamas-orchestrated; the Hamas link remained suspected [S5].

diamond.adversary: Arabic-speaking, politically motivated operators believed by Talos to operate from Gaza; suspected Hamas alignment [S2][S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Micropsia, BarbWire, SpyC23 and AridSpy malware; phishing, catfishing and trojanized apps [S3][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C&C servers; third-party app download sites rather than Google Play [S6]. Cybereason found Bearded Barbie infrastructure largely separate from known APT-C-23 infrastructure [S4].
diamond.victim: Palestinian, Israeli and Egyptian government, military, law-enforcement, activist and civilian Android users [S2][S3][S4][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Israeli-Palestinian conflict and Palestinian factional rivalry; Cybereason suggested Hamas-Fatah rivalry may help explain targeting of Palestinians [S4][S5].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, Android devices, social media platforms (Facebook) and messaging apps [S3][S4][S6].

gaps: No Microsoft-authored report on Pinstripe Lightning was retrieved; the Microsoft-to-Arid Viper mapping rests on Microsoft's naming feed [S1]. Microsoft's own scope, confidence and origin for this name are unknown.
Hamas sponsorship is suspected, not confirmed [S5]. No government attribution was found.
Cluster boundary with Molerats / Gaza Cybergang and APT-C-23 is disputed across vendors [S4][S5].

Web fetches to vendor and Malpedia pages failed in this session, so findings rely on search-result summaries; primary pages (Kaspersky, Talos, Cybereason, ESET, SentinelOne) should be opened and verified.
SentinelOne publication date is given as 2023-10 from context and not read from the page [S5].
Activity after June 2024 and any Microsoft-observed activity are not covered.
No ATT&CK group ID is mapped in this record.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is personal Android devices, social media accounts and messaging apps of defense, law-enforcement and government personnel, plus Windows endpoints used for Palestinian or regional political work [S4][S6]. STEP 2: The actor relies on social engineering rather than exploits, and distributes apps outside official stores [S3][S6]. STEP 3: Pattern is themed lure or fake persona, then downloader or trojanized app, then backdoor or spyware with data theft [S3][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against Palestinian, Israeli and Egyptian targets, tracking regional events [S3][S6]. MDCOA is catfishing of deployed or regional military and coalition personnel to gain device access. Candidate indicators: sideloaded APKs from third-party sites, unexpected Facebook contacts shifting to other apps, RAR attachments from social contacts, Delphi-built executables with political decoy documents [S3][S4][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track mobile and social-media compromise vectors for personnel in the Middle East, not only network intrusions [S4][S6]. (2) Authorities: personal-device monitoring and reporting channels need clear authority and policy before use. (3) Mission assurance: personnel awareness and sideloading restrictions on government-issued mobile devices reduce exposure [S6]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners and vendors, noting that cluster naming (Arid Viper, APT-C-23, Molerats) differs by source [S4][S5].
